briefing.headline: Without this, you lose work. With it, you can ship.
body: Git tracks every change to every file in a project. GitHub stores those changes online so you can share, collaborate, or recover when your laptop dies. They're separate things that work together — Git is the tool, GitHub is the host.

This is the one module you can't fake. Ship a real project without Git and you'll lose work eventually. Lose work once and you'll never not use Git again. The good news: 90% of daily Git is six commands. Get those, and the rest is reference.

reference.title: The daily six
reference.content:
git status                     What's changed?
git add <file>                 Stage a file for commit
git add .                      Stage everything
git commit -m "<message>"      Save staged changes
git push                       Send commits to GitHub
git pull                       Get latest from GitHub

reference.title: The three states
reference.content:
Every file in a Git repo lives in one of three states.
Working directory — files as they are on disk right now.
Staging area — files you've added with git add, marked for the next commit.
Committed — saved permanently in Git's history.

reference.title: Branches
reference.content:
git branch                     List branches
git branch <name>              Create a branch
git switch <name>              Switch to a branch
git switch -c <name>           Create and switch in one
git merge <name>               Merge <name> into current
git branch -d <name>           Delete a merged branch

reference.title: When you mess up
reference.content:
git commit --amend           Edit the last commit
git restore <file>           Undo unstaged changes to a file
git restore --staged <file>  Unstage a file
git revert <hash>            Make a new commit that undoes an old one
git reset --hard HEAD        DANGER: throw away all uncommitted changes

reference.title: What goes in .gitignore
reference.content: Anything you don't want tracked: node_modules/, .env, .DS_Store, build outputs (dist/, build/), editor settings (.vscode/), log files. The rule: if it's regenerated automatically or contains secrets, ignore it.

reference.title: "fatal: not a git repository"
reference.content: You're not inside a git-initialized folder. Run pwd to see where you are, then cd into the project root — or run git init if this is a new project.

reference.title: "Permission denied (publickey)" on push
reference.content: Your SSH key isn't set up correctly with GitHub. Run ssh -T git@github.com to test — if it doesn't say Hi <username>!, redo the SSH key step.

completion.headline: M3 complete.
completion.body: You can track changes, branch, push to GitHub, and recover from mistakes. Phase 1 is done. Next up: M4 — JavaScript for Directors.

steps.title: Configure your identity
steps.body: Every commit Git makes is signed with a name and email. Set them once, globally — they apply to every repo on this machine. Use the same email you'll use for GitHub, otherwise GitHub won't attribute your commits to your profile.
steps.tryCue: Run all four. They write to ~/.gitconfig.
steps.code:
git config --global user.name "Your Name"
git config --global user.email "you@example.com"
git config --global init.defaultBranch main
git config --global pull.rebase false

commandNotes.what: Your identity on every commit, on this machine, in every repo unless overridden per-repo.
commandNotes.when: First time setting up a new Mac. Also the first thing to check if git commit errors with Please tell me who you are, or if commits show the wrong author on GitHub.

commandNotes.what: Makes new repos start on main instead of the legacy master.
commandNotes.when: Standard everywhere now — GitHub, GitLab, every modern codebase uses main. Without this setting, git init creates a master branch and you'll have to rename it.

commandNotes.what: Tells git pull to merge remote changes (the default behavior) rather than rebase. Predictable, beginner-friendly.
commandNotes.when: Stops Git from nagging with hint: Pulling without specifying how to reconcile divergent branches the first time you git pull with local changes.

whenYoullReachForThis: Setting up a new Mac — these are the first commands before any git init or git clone
Switching email for a work account on the same machine — git config user.email (without --global) sets it per-repo
Commits showing the wrong author on GitHub — check git config --global user.email matches your GitHub email
Cloning a repo on a fresh machine and the very first git commit errors with "Please tell me who you are"

steps.title: Make your first repo
steps.body: git init turns any folder into a Git repository. It creates a hidden .git/ directory that stores all the version history — every change, every commit message, every author. The folder is otherwise normal; you can still work with it from Finder, VS Code, or the terminal.
steps.tryCue: Run all five. Watch what ls -la reveals after git init.
steps.code:
cd ~
mkdir mve-git-practice
cd mve-git-practice
git init
ls -la

commandNotes.what: Creates a new Git repository in the current directory by making a .git/ subfolder. Doesn't touch any other files.
commandNotes.when: Starting a brand-new project that doesn't exist on GitHub yet. Or adopting an existing folder into Git — cd into it, git init, add a .gitignore, commit.

commandNotes.what: Long listing with hidden files. Reveals the new .git/ directory.
commandNotes.when: Confirming a folder is actually a Git repo without running git status. Or curious what hidden files a project tracks — .env, .github/, .gitignore.

steps.verify: ls -la shows a .git directory. Run git status — it says On branch main and No commits yet.
whenYoullReachForThis: Starting any new local project before pushing it to GitHub
Putting an old un-tracked folder under version control — cd in, git init, add a .gitignore, commit
Setting up a scratch repo to test a Git command without risking a real project
After accidentally deleting .git/ — git init starts fresh, but all history is gone

steps.title: The commit loop
steps.body: The basic Git rhythm: change a file, git status to see what's changed, git add to stage, git commit to save. You'll do this hundreds of times per project. Most of Git is variations on this loop.
steps.tryCue: Run all six. Read each git status output carefully — the state changes between them.
steps.code:
echo "# MVE Git Practice" > README.md
git status
git add README.md
git status
git commit -m "Add README"
git status

commandNotes.what: Shows what's changed since the last commit, what's staged, and what's untracked.
commandNotes.when: The most-run Git command, period. Before every git add to confirm what you're about to stage. Before every commit to confirm what's in it.

commandNotes.what: Stages the file for the next commit — moves it into Git's "staging area" without committing yet.
commandNotes.when: You've edited several files and only want to commit some of them. git add <file> stages just that one; git add . stages everything in the working directory.

commandNotes.what: Snapshots the staged changes with a message. The message becomes part of the project's permanent history.
commandNotes.when: Every time you have a logical chunk of work complete. Good messages describe what changed in the imperative: Add login form, not Added login form or Login form changes.

steps.verify: Final git status shows: nothing to commit, working tree clean.
steps.trouble: If commit errors with Please tell me who you are: you skipped Step 1. Run those config commands, then retry the commit.
whenYoullReachForThis: Every commit you ever make follows this loop — status, add, commit
Reviewing what you're about to commit before pushing — git status followed by git diff --staged
Cherry-picking which changes to include — git add some files, leave others uncommitted
Saving work mid-task before switching branches or stepping away — even a rough commit beats losing changes
After Claude Code modifies several files — git status tells you what changed before you decide whether to keep it

steps.title: View history and diffs
steps.body: git log shows the commit history — newest first. --oneline compresses it to one commit per line. git diff shows what's changed since the last commit, before you stage anything. These three commands answer most "what happened?" questions.
steps.tryCue: Run all six. git diff output should match what you just added.
steps.code:
echo "" >> README.md
echo "Practice repo for Git basics." >> README.md
git diff
git add README.md
git commit -m "Add description to README"
git log --oneline

commandNotes.what: Shows unstaged changes line by line. Added lines in green with +, removed in red with -.
commandNotes.when: Before git add, to confirm what you actually changed. After Claude Code edits a file, to see exactly what it did before you stage it.

commandNotes.what: Same as git diff but shows what's already staged — what's about to be committed.
commandNotes.when: Right before git commit, as a last sanity check. "Am I about to commit what I think I'm committing?"

commandNotes.what: Compact commit history — one line per commit, with the short hash and message.
commandNotes.when: Skimming recent history to find when something changed. The full git log is too verbose for fast reading; --oneline is the daily form.

steps.verify: git diff showed your new lines (in green, with + in front). git log --oneline shows two commits.
whenYoullReachForThis: Reviewing what you changed before committing — git diff
Finding the commit where a bug was introduced — git log --oneline to scan, then git show <hash>
Checking what a teammate did since you last pulled — git log --oneline origin/main..HEAD
Debugging "what did Claude Code actually change?" — git diff right after it finishes
Confirming a refactor didn't sneak in unintended changes — git diff --staged before commit

steps.title: Add a .gitignore
steps.body: A .gitignore file tells Git which paths to never track. Anything regenerated automatically (node_modules/), anything with secrets (.env), and anything macOS scatters into every folder (.DS_Store) belongs here. Without one, you'll eventually commit a 200MB node_modules or an API key.
steps.tryCue: Run all seven. The proof: does git status ignore .DS_Store?
steps.code:
echo ".DS_Store" > .gitignore
echo "node_modules/" >> .gitignore
echo ".env" >> .gitignore
touch .DS_Store
git status
git add .gitignore
git commit -m "Add .gitignore"

commandNotes.what: macOS metadata file Finder creates in every folder it opens. Useless on other systems; pure noise in a repo.
commandNotes.when: Every repo on macOS needs this in .gitignore. Otherwise Finder leaves one for you every time you open the folder.

commandNotes.what: Trailing slash means "this directory and everything inside it." node_modules/ is regenerated by npm install from package.json — there's no reason to track it.
commandNotes.when: Every JavaScript project. Skipping this is the most common way new repos balloon to gigabytes.

commandNotes.what: The conventional filename for environment variables — API keys, database URLs, secrets.
commandNotes.when: Always. Committing .env is how API keys end up in public GitHub repos and how cloud bills hit five digits before anyone notices.

steps.verify: Before the commit, git status showed .gitignore as a new file but did not show .DS_Store — Git is correctly ignoring it. After the commit, git log --oneline shows three commits.
whenYoullReachForThis: Starting any new project — .gitignore goes in before your first git add
Adopting a project that doesn't have one — symptom is git status listing node_modules or .DS_Store as changes
Adding a new tool that creates a build folder (dist/, .next/, build/) — add it to .gitignore right then
After accidentally committing a secret — add to .gitignore, then git rm --cached <file>, then rotate the secret

steps.title: Branches
steps.body: A branch is an independent line of work. You start on main. When you want to try something without risking the working version — a feature, an experiment, a refactor — you make a branch. Switch to it, make changes there, leave main alone. If it works, you merge it back. If not, you delete the branch and nothing ever happened to main.
steps.tryCue: Run all seven. The final cat proves the branches are independent.
steps.code:
git switch -c experiment
echo "Trying something new." >> README.md
git add README.md
git commit -m "Try a new line"
git log --oneline
git switch main
cat README.md

commandNotes.what: Create a new branch and switch to it in one command. -c stands for "create."
commandNotes.when: Starting any unit of work bigger than a typo fix — a new feature, a refactor, an experiment. Especially anywhere you might want to throw the work away cleanly.

commandNotes.what: Switch back to main without creating anything. Your working directory updates to match main.
commandNotes.when: Returning to the known-good version after an experiment didn't pan out. Or jumping back to fix an unrelated bug while a feature branch is in flight.

commandNotes.what: Commit history of the current branch.
commandNotes.when: Confirming a commit landed where you expected — sometimes you commit thinking you're on feature/x and you're actually on main.

steps.verify: After switching back to main, cat README.md doesn't show Trying something new. — that line only exists on the experiment branch.
whenYoullReachForThis: Trying a refactor or new feature you're not sure will work — branch off, experiment, throw it away if it doesn't pan out
Pull request workflow — every PR is a branch off main
Hot-fixing a bug while a long feature branch is in flight — git switch main, branch off, fix, merge, switch back
Letting Claude Code experiment on a branch so you can review the diff before merging into main
Pairing on a project — each person works on their own branch and merges to main when ready

steps.title: Merge a branch
steps.body: Merging takes commits from one branch and applies them to another. To bring experiment's changes into main, switch to main first, then merge. After a successful merge, the experiment branch has done its job — delete it so the branch list doesn't pile up.
steps.tryCue: Run all five. cat README.md should now show the line from experiment.
steps.code:
git switch main
git merge experiment
cat README.md
git log --oneline
git branch -d experiment

commandNotes.what: Brings commits from <branch> into the branch you're currently on. Always run from the destination branch — "I'm on main, merge experiment into me."
commandNotes.when: Bringing a finished feature branch into main. In larger teams, this happens via a pull request on GitHub instead of locally — but the underlying operation is the same.

commandNotes.what: Deletes a branch that's already been merged. The -d protects you — Git refuses if there are unmerged commits.
commandNotes.when: Right after merging a feature branch. Leaving merged branches around clutters git branch output and confuses future you.

steps.verify: README.md now contains the new line. git log --oneline shows the experiment commit on main. git branch shows only main.
whenYoullReachForThis: Finishing a feature on a branch — switch to main, merge, delete the branch
Pulling a teammate's changes after their PR was merged on GitHub — git switch main, git pull (which is fetch + merge)
Resolving a merge conflict — Git stops mid-merge, you edit the conflicting files, git add, git commit
Cleaning up after a sprint — list merged branches with git branch --merged, delete the dead ones

steps.title: Create a GitHub account
steps.body: Skip if you already have one. Otherwise: github.com → Sign up. Use the same email you used in git config — otherwise GitHub won't attribute your commits to your profile.
notes: Pick a username you can live with — it'll be in the URL of every public repo you ever make.
Verify your email when GitHub sends the link.
You don't need GitHub Pro. Free is fine for everything in this course.
steps.verify: You can sign in to github.com and see your dashboard.

steps.title: Generate an SSH key
steps.body: SSH keys let your Mac authenticate to GitHub without typing a password every time. You generate a matched pair — a private key that stays on your machine forever and a public key you give to GitHub. The public one is safe to share. The private one is not. When prompted for a file location, press Enter to accept the default. When prompted for a passphrase, press Enter twice for none — or set one if you prefer.
steps.tryCue: Run it. Press Enter through the prompts.

commandNotes.what: Generates an SSH key pair. Default location: ~/.ssh/.
commandNotes.when: Setting up a new Mac. Or adding a new identity for a separate account (work vs. personal GitHub). Or rotating keys if you suspect one was leaked.

commandNotes.what: Sets the key type. Ed25519 is the modern default — shorter and faster than the older RSA.
commandNotes.when: Always for new keys. RSA still works but there's no reason to pick it for new keys in 2026.

commandNotes.what: Comment field embedded in the public key. Just a label — usually your email — that helps you identify the key later.
commandNotes.when: Telling keys apart on a machine with several — work GitHub key, personal GitHub key, server access key. The comment shows up at the end of the public key file.

whenYoullReachForThis: Setting up a new Mac — first thing before git push will work
Adding access to a remote server you SSH into — the same public key gets pasted into ~/.ssh/authorized_keys there
Rotating keys after suspecting one was compromised — generate a new pair, replace the public key in GitHub, delete the old private key
Setting up a second GitHub identity (work + personal on the same machine) — second key, custom filename, configured in ~/.ssh/config

steps.title: Add the SSH key to GitHub
steps.body: Copy your public key and paste it into GitHub. The public one ends in .pub — never share the one without .pub.
steps.tryCue: Run this first — it copies your public key to the clipboard.

commandNotes.what: Reads from stdin and copies to the macOS clipboard. The < redirects the file's contents into pbcopy.
commandNotes.when: Piping any command's output into the clipboard. git log --oneline | pbcopy grabs a commit list. cat file.txt | pbcopy copies a whole file.

notes: Go to github.com → click your avatar (top right) → Settings.
SSH and GPG keys in the left sidebar.
New SSH key. Title it something like "MacBook". Paste into the Key field. Save.
steps.verify: Run ssh -T git@github.com in iTerm2. It says Hi <your-username>! You've successfully authenticated.
steps.trouble: If it says The authenticity of host 'github.com' can't be established — type yes and press Enter. That's a one-time confirmation.
whenYoullReachForThis: Setting up GitHub access on a new Mac — generate key, pbcopy, paste in GitHub
Adding a second machine to your GitHub account — same flow, separate key per machine, named after the machine
Setting up SSH for any other host that supports it (a server, GitLab, Bitbucket) — same pattern, different paste destination
Diagnosing "Permission denied (publickey)" — confirm a key in ~/.ssh/ matches one in your GitHub settings

steps.title: Push to GitHub
steps.body: Create a repo on GitHub, link it to your local repo, push your commits up. On github.com, click + (top right) → New repository. Name it mve-git-practice. Don't add a README, .gitignore, or license — your local repo already has them. Click Create repository. GitHub then shows a setup page with an SSH URL (starts with git@github.com:). Copy that URL — you'll paste it into the command below.
steps.tryCue: Replace YOUR_USERNAME with yours, then run both lines from your mve-git-practice folder.
steps.code:
git remote add origin git@github.com:YOUR_USERNAME/mve-git-practice.git
git push -u origin main

commandNotes.what: Adds a named remote — a shortcut for a URL. origin is the conventional name for the primary remote (usually GitHub).
commandNotes.when: First push of any new local repo to GitHub. Done once per repo — after that, git push already knows where to send commits.

commandNotes.what: Push main to origin, and set origin/main as the upstream. -u means future git push from this branch needs no arguments.
commandNotes.when: First push of any new branch — the -u sets the tracking relationship. Without it, future pushes need git push origin main spelled out every time.

steps.verify: Refresh the GitHub repo page. Your README, .gitignore, and three commits are visible.
whenYoullReachForThis: Pushing a brand-new local repo to GitHub for the first time — these two commands, every time
Adding a second remote (a fork, a deploy target) — git remote add <name> <url> with a name other than origin
After the first push, just git push works — no arguments needed once the upstream is set
Switching a repo to a new GitHub account or org — git remote set-url origin <new-url>

steps.title: Edit on GitHub, pull locally
steps.body: Simulate the situation where the remote has changes you don't. Edit a file directly in GitHub's web UI, then pull those changes down. On the GitHub repo page, click README.md. Click the pencil icon (top right of the file view) to edit. Add a new line. Click Commit changes at the top right, then Commit changes again in the dialog.
steps.tryCue: Then back in iTerm2, run all three.
steps.code:
git pull
cat README.md
git log --oneline

commandNotes.what: Fetches commits from the remote and merges them into the current branch. fetch + merge in one command.
commandNotes.when: Starting work on a project after someone else (or web-UI you) has pushed changes. Run it as your first move when sitting down at a shared repo.

steps.verify: README.md contains the line you added on GitHub. git log --oneline shows the new commit.
whenYoullReachForThis: Starting a project session after a teammate pushed overnight — git pull is the first command
Working on a repo across two machines — push from one, pull from the other
After editing via GitHub's web UI (quick fix to a README, a single-line PR change) — git pull to sync local
Resolving a divergent local branch — Git stops mid-pull, you fix conflicts, commit, finish the merge

steps.title: Undo: amend the last commit
steps.body: Two things go wrong often: you commit and realize you forgot to include a file, or you spot a typo in the commit message the instant after you save it. --amend fixes both — it replaces the last commit with a new one, no additional "oops" commit polluting history. The constraint: only safe before you push. Amending a commit that's already on GitHub rewrites history that may have already been pulled.
steps.tryCue: Run all four. The commit count stays the same; the most recent hash changes.
steps.code:
echo "One more line." >> README.md
git add README.md
git commit --amend --no-edit
git log --oneline

commandNotes.what: Replaces the last commit with a new one that includes your currently-staged changes. Opens the message editor by default.
commandNotes.when: You committed and immediately realized you forgot to add a file — git add <missing-file>, then git commit --amend. Or you want to fix a typo in the last commit message.

commandNotes.what: Skip opening the message editor — keep the existing commit message.
commandNotes.when: You're just adding a forgotten file to the last commit and don't want to change the message. Without --no-edit, Git opens vim and waits for you to save.

steps.verify: git log --oneline shows the same number of commits as before the amend. The most recent commit's hash has changed — that's the rewrite.
steps.trouble: If you've already pushed and then amend, the next git push will be rejected with "Updates were rejected." You can force it with git push --force-with-lease, but never do that on a shared branch.
whenYoullReachForThis: Spotting a typo in the commit message you just made — git commit --amend rewrites the message
Forgetting to git add a file before committing — git add it, then git commit --amend --no-edit
Tidying up a commit before the first push — better to amend than to leave a "fix typo" commit cluttering history
Working on a personal branch nobody else pulls from — amend freely; the constraint only matters on shared branches

steps.title: Clean up
steps.body: Delete the practice folder locally. Optionally delete the GitHub repo too (Settings → scroll to bottom → Delete this repository).
